title: Harness Engineering: How to Build Software When Humans Steer, Agents Execute — Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is building software exclusively with coding agents, covering harness design, reviewer agents, and agent-driven engineering workflows. The content is about coding assistants and the developer platform infrastructure (skills, lints, CI agents) that supports agent-driven development. The discussion centers on production deployment of coding agents in daily engineering workflows with CI integration and operational practices. The talk assumes deep familiarity with software engineering, CI/CD, agent operations, and harness design, targeting experienced practitioners. This is a keynote talk with a post-keynote Q&A session. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript, directly quoting the speaker's statements.

summary: Ryan Lopopolo introduces "Harness Engineering"—building software where humans steer and agents execute. Over nine months, his team has built software exclusively with agents, banning direct editor use. His central thesis: code is now free and infinitely abundant; implementation is no longer the scarce resource. The scarce resources are human time, human and model attention, and model context window. GPT 5.2 marked the inflection point where models became isomorphic to human engineers in code production quality. The engineer's role shifts to specifying non-functional requirements—documenting what good work looks like through breadcrumbs, ADRs, persona-oriented documentation, and historical logs. Lopopolo describes using reviewer agents in CI for security and reliability checks, bespoke lints to durably eliminate recurring failure classes, and tests that assert code structure (e.g., file length limits) to adapt codebases to model context constraints. He emphasizes that everything is a prompt—lint messages, rules files, skills, review agent comments—and that leverage stacks across repository, team, and agents. QA plans document features and critical user journeys, enabling review agents to assert completion criteria. In Q&A, Lopopolo describes his workflow: starting from tickets, giving agents skills that teach them to launch apps, spin up observability stacks, and attach debuggers. The team centralizes leverage around five to ten skills. He addresses over-engineering by invoking the bitter lesson: do minimum context management, surfacing instructions just-in-time at lint or test time. He favors first-party harnesses like Codex because labs post-train models in the context of their harnesses. Collaboration centers on markdown files and GitHub PRs, treating PRs as a hub-and-spoke broadcast domain where agents can acknowledge, defer, or reject feedback. For code review at velocity, the team designated Fridays as "garbage collection day" to categorically eliminate recurring slop, closing the loop between human feedback and repository guardrails. Reviewer agents are bucketed by persona (front-end architect, reliability engineer, scalability), triggered on every push. Token usage splits roughly into thirds: planning/ticket curation/documentation, implementation, and CI. Lopopolo treats plans cautiously—if used, they should be single PRs with human review before execution, since unread plans encode unwanted instructions. He embraces the mental model of LLMs as fuzzy compilers, with harness engineering constraints acting like static analysis and optimization passes. His future vision: hand agents a token budget, ranked priorities, and success/reliability metrics for a quarter or year, letting them continuously advance the product without human hands on the wheel. As code production automates away, his attention shifts to triaging user feedback, ensuring no PII leaks, monitoring user sentiment, and supporting operations staff with runbooks—meta-programming the processes and acceptance criteria for agents to execute.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Code is free and infinitely abundant; implementation is no longer the scarce resource—human time, attention, and context window are.
Everything in harness engineering is a prompt—lint messages, rules files, skills, review agent comments—none requiring weight changes.
Favor first-party harnesses like Codex because labs post-train models in the context of their harness, providing leverage better ridden than rebuilt.
Treat PRs as a hub-and-spoke broadcast domain where agents can acknowledge, defer, or reject feedback; being too prescriptive causes agents to be bullied by reviewers.

LLM as fuzzy compiler is a useful mental model: harness engineering constraints are like static analysis and optimization passes that limit which generated code is acceptable.

Every human interaction with an agent is a harness failure; the goal is agents running 24/7 with zero human intervention.

sections.title: Introduction and Core Thesis
sections.summary: Lopopolo introduces himself and his experience building software exclusively with agents for nine months. He presents the core thesis: code is free, implementation is no longer scarce, and every engineer has access to massive parallel capacity constrained only by GPU and token budgets. He frames the shift toward systems thinking and delegation.

sections.title: The AGI-Pilled Worldview and Scarce Resources
sections.summary: Lopopolo identifies GPT 5.2 as the turning point where models became isomorphic to human engineers. He enumerates the three scarce resources: human time, human and model attention, and model context window. He contrasts the old P0/P2 stack-rank world with the new world where even P3 tasks get kicked off immediately in parallel.

sections.title: Making Work Legible to Agents
sections.summary: Lopopolo argues that the important thing is not the code but the prompts, guardrails, and documentation that produced it. He emphasizes breadcrumbs, ADRs, persona-oriented documentation, and making codebases native to agents. He highlights that large-scale refactoring is now free and migrations can be completed by firing off many parallel agents.

sections.title: Non-Functional Requirements and Doing a Good Job
sections.summary: Lopopolo explains that a single patch involves hundreds of decisions about non-functional requirements. The models have seen trillions of lines of code making every possible choice, so engineers must specify what good looks like. He advocates taking short-term velocity hits to diagnose and guardrail agent failures, then stepping back to higher-leverage work.

sections.title: Tooling Techniques and Durable Failure Elimination
sections.summary: Lopopolo describes tools for keeping agents on track: agents.md files, auto-compaction in GPT-5.4 and Codex, reviewer agents in CI for security and reliability, and bespoke lints. He gives the example of durably solving missing timeouts and retries on network code by writing a custom lint, leveraging the axiom that code is free to migrate the entire codebase once and for all.

sections.title: Tests, Prompts, and QA Plans as Leverage
sections.summary: Lopopolo describes writing structural tests (e.g., file length limits) to adapt codebases to model context constraints. He emphasizes that everything is a prompt—lint messages, rules files, skills, review agent comments—and that leverage stacks across repository, team, and agents. He describes using agent SDKs embedded in tests to review code acceptability, and using agents to synthesize prompt-writing skills. QA plans documenting features and critical user journeys enable review agents to assert completion criteria, increasing trust and reducing human oversight.

sections.title: Q&A Introduction and Workflow Setup
sections.summary: Vibhu Sapra introduces the Q&A, noting Lopopolo's Latent Space episode and his spending of over a billion output tokens daily. Lopopolo describes his workflow: starting from tickets, giving agents skills that teach them to launch apps, spin up observability stacks, and attach Chrome DevTools. The team centralizes leverage around five to ten skills, hiding infrastructure complexity beneath them. He notes an infrastructure change went unnoticed for three weeks because skills abstracted it.

sections.title: Over-Engineering Harnesses and the Bitter Lesson
sections.summary: Lopopolo addresses avoiding over-engineering harnesses by invoking the bitter lesson: do the minimum context management to surface instructions at the right time. Context management won't be obsoleted since models must always be told task requirements and guardrails. He advocates just-in-time instruction surfacing—letting agents prototype and experiment, then enforcing structural requirements at lint or test time rather than front-loading instructions. This approach survives model capability increases.

sections.title: First-Party Harnesses and Collaboration Practices
sections.summary: Lopopolo advocates using first-party harnesses like Codex because labs post-train models in the context of their harness, providing leverage better ridden than rebuilt. He describes collaboration centered on markdown files and GitHub PRs treated as a hub-and-spoke broadcast domain where agents and humans participate without blocking. Agents can acknowledge, defer, or reject feedback, avoiding the failure mode of being bullied by reviewers. He biases toward code being accepted, not perfect.

sections.title: Getting Started with Coding Agents
sections.summary: Lopopolo offers two paths for engineers transitioning to agents: use agents to write tests improving confidence in existing code (which also improves agent navigability), and audit time spent on manual tasks to incrementally automate them. He emphasizes the high-leverage parts of the job are defining, prioritizing, scheduling, and delegating work, paralleling team management principles.

sections.title: Car Workflow and Zero-Interaction Goal
sections.summary: Lopopolo describes kicking off tasks before leaving the office, tethering his laptop to his phone, and letting agents cook during his 30-minute commute with skills that run until tests are green. His dream is 50 agents running 24/7 with zero interaction, stating that every time he has to type continue to the agent is a harness failure to provide enough context for completion.

sections.title: Scaling Repositories and Code Review at Velocity
sections.summary: Lopopolo describes restructuring from a blank monorepo into 750 PNPM workspace packages isolated by domain, enforcing one canonical way to do everything (one ORM, one language, one CI style) for transferable agent context. For high-velocity code review, the team designated Fridays as garbage collection day to categorically eliminate recurring slop that made PRs hard to merge, closing the loop between human feedback and repository guardrails. With three to five PRs per engineer per day on a team of three, merge conflicts drove both architectural tree-out and faster merge cycles.

sections.title: Self-Healing Agents and Persona-Based Review
sections.summary: Lopopolo describes automatically prompt-injecting agents to self-heal when they produce bad behavior, converting synchronous human review feedback into documentation that is surfaced via failing tests or reviewer agents. The team bucketed review feedback by persona—front-end architect, reliability engineer, scalability—and spun up persona-specific review agents triggered on every push, continuously appending to documentation files to progressively reduce slop.

sections.title: Token Budget Allocation and Plan Mode
sections.summary: Lopopolo estimates token usage splits roughly into thirds: planning/ticket curation/documentation, implementation, and CI. He expresses skepticism about plan mode, preferring to drop tickets directly without diverting through plans he won't read. If plans are used, he recommends pushing them as single PRs with full human review before execution, since approving unread plans encodes unwanted instructions. He emphasizes that spending tokens in CI is necessary because getting code accepted, not writing it, is the hard part.

sections.title: Code as Disposable Build Artifact and LLM as Fuzzy Compiler
sections.summary: Lopopolo confirms code is a disposable build artifact, referencing Symphony, an agent orchestrator treating a library as a well-defined spec with code as compiled output. He proposes the mental model of LLMs as fuzzy compilers, where harness engineering constraints act like static analysis and optimization passes that determine which generated code is acceptable—analogous to LLVM optimization passes in Rust compilation. Swapping models is like changing the code generation backend; the structural rules ensure acceptable output regardless.

sections.title: Future Vision: Autonomous Agent-Driven Engineering
sections.summary: Lopopolo describes his future vision: handing agents a token budget and a quarter or year of ranked work with success and reliability metrics, letting them continuously advance the product without human intervention. As software progresses through prototyping to alpha and beta, new engineering capabilities emerge from zero and must be built up—like pentagonal capability charts. Beyond writing code, engineering includes triaging user feedback, preventing PII leaks, monitoring sentiment, and writing runbooks for operations staff. As agents handle code production, the engineer's role shifts to meta-programming these processes and acceptance criteria.
